question.:question/problem: Let $f(x,y)={x}^{3}+y.$ Given that $C$ is the path along the curve $r(t)=⟨3t,{t}^{3}⟩$ for $t\in [0,1],$ evaluate ${\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $C$ be a piecewise-smooth curve given by the vector function $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b].$ Let $f$ be a differentiable function of two or three variables such that $∇f$ is continuous on $C.$ The fundamental theorem for line integrals states that 

$$
{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r=f(r(b))-f(r(a)).
$$

 

In our case, the position vectors of the endpoints of the curve are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨0,0⟩ \\ r(1) & =⟨3,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the endpoints of the path defined by $C$ are $(0,0)$ and $(3,1).$

Applying the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r & =f(r(1))-f(r(0))  \\  & =f(3,1)-f(0,0)  \\  & =({3}^{3}+1)-({0}^{3}+0)  \\  & =(27+1)-0  \\  & =28.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $C$ be a piecewise-smooth curve given by the vector function $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b].$ Let $f$ be a differentiable function of two or three variables such that $∇f$ is continuous on $C.$ The fundamental theorem for line integrals states that 

$$
{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r=f(r(b))-f(r(a)).
$$

 

In our case, the position vectors of the endpoints of the curve are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨0,0⟩ \\ r(\pi) & =⟨\pi,6⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the endpoints of the path defined by $C$ are $(0,0)$ and $(\pi,6).$

Applying the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r & =f(r(\pi))-f(r(0)) \\  & =f(\pi,6)-f(0,0) \\  & =\left(\left(\pi\right)^{2} \left(6\right) - \left(\pi\right) \left(6\right)^{2}\right)-\left(\left(0\right)^{2} \left(0\right) - \left(0\right) \left(0\right)^{2}\right) \\  & =\left(- 36 \pi + 6 \pi^{2}\right)-\left(0\right) \\  & =- 36 \pi + 6 \pi^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

question.:question/problem: Let $f(x,y)=2 y e^{2 x}.$ Given that $C$ is the path along the curve $r(t)=⟨t,3 t^{2}⟩$ for $t\in [0,1],$ evaluate ${\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $C$ be a piecewise-smooth curve given by the vector function $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b].$ Let $f$ be a differentiable function of two or three variables such that $∇f$ is continuous on $C.$ The fundamental theorem for line integrals states that 

$$
{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r=f(r(b))-f(r(a)).
$$

 

In our case, the position vectors of the endpoints of the curve are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨0,0⟩ \\ r(1) & =⟨1,3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the endpoints of the path defined by $C$ are $(0,0)$ and $(1,3).$

Applying the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r & =f(r(1))-f(r(0)) \\  & =f(1,3)-f(0,0) \\  & =\left(2 \left(3\right) e^{2 \left(1\right)}\right)-\left(2 \left(0\right) e^{2 \left(0\right)}\right) \\  & =\left(6 e^{2}\right)-\left(0\right) \\  & =6 e^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $C$ be a piecewise-smooth curve given by the vector function $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b].$ Let $f$ be a differentiable function of two or three variables such that $∇f$ is continuous on $C.$ The fundamental theorem for line integrals states that 

$$
{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r=f(r(b))-f(r(a)).
$$

 

In our case, the position vectors of the endpoints of the curve are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨0,0⟩ \\ r(1) & =⟨1,2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the endpoints of the path defined by $C$ are $(0,0)$ and $(1,2).$

Applying the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r & =f(r(1))-f(r(0)) \\  & =f(1,2)-f(0,0) \\  & =\left(3 \left(2\right) e^{3 \left(1\right)}\right)-\left(3 \left(0\right) e^{3 \left(0\right)}\right) \\  & =\left(6 e^{3}\right)-\left(0\right) \\  & =6 e^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $C$ be a piecewise-smooth curve given by the vector function $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b].$ Let $f$ be a differentiable function of two or three variables such that $∇f$ is continuous on $C.$ The fundamental theorem for line integrals states that 

$$
{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r=f(r(b))-f(r(a)).
$$

 

In our case, the position vectors of the endpoints of the curve are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(\frac{\pi}{2}) & =⟨\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{3 \pi}{2}⟩ \\ r(\pi) & =⟨\pi,3 \pi⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the endpoints of the path defined by $C$ are $(\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{3 \pi}{2})$ and $(\pi,3 \pi).$

Applying the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r & =f(r(\pi))-f(r(\frac{\pi}{2})) \\  & =f(\pi,3 \pi)-f(\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{3 \pi}{2}) \\  & =\left(2 \left(\pi\right) + 2 \left(3 \pi\right) \cos{\left(\left(\pi\right) \right)}\right)-\left(2 \left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right) + 2 \left(\frac{3 \pi}{2}\right) \cos{\left(\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right) \right)}\right) \\  & =\left(- 4 \pi\right)-\left(\pi\right) \\  & =- 5 \pi.\end{aligned}

question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $C$ be a piecewise-smooth curve given by the vector function $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b].$ Let $f$ be a differentiable function of two or three variables such that $∇f$ is continuous on $C.$ The fundamental theorem for line integrals states that 

$$
{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r=f(r(b))-f(r(a)).
$$

 

In our case, the position vectors of the endpoints of the curve are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨0,0,0⟩ \\ r(\frac{\pi}{2}) & =⟨2,\frac{\pi}{2},\pi⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the endpoints of the path defined by $C$ are $(0,0,0)$ and $(2,\frac{\pi}{2},\pi).$

Applying the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r & =f(r(\frac{\pi}{2}))-f(r(0)) \\  & =f(2,\frac{\pi}{2},\pi)-f(0,0,0) \\  & =\left(2 \left(2\right) \sin{\left(\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right) \right)} + 2 \left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right) \cos{\left(\left(\pi\right) \right)}\right)-\left(2 \left(0\right) \sin{\left(\left(0\right) \right)} + 2 \left(0\right) \cos{\left(\left(0\right) \right)}\right) \\  & =2\left(\left(2+\frac{\pi}{2}\cdot\left(-1\right)\right)-\left(0\right)\right) \\  & =4 - \pi.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r=f(r(b))-f(r(a)).

In our case, the position vectors of the endpoints of the curve are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨0,0,0⟩ \\ r(1) & =⟨1,1,3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the endpoints of the path defined by $C$ are $(0,0,0)$ and $(1,1,3).$

Applying the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r & =f(r(1))-f(r(0)) \\  & =f(1,1,3)-f(0,0,0) \\  & =\left(- 2 e^{\left(1\right)} - 2 e^{\left(1\right)} - 2 e^{\left(3\right)}\right)-\left(- 2 e^{\left(0\right)} - 2 e^{\left(0\right)} - 2 e^{\left(0\right)}\right) \\  & =\left(- 2 e^{3} - 4 e\right)-\left(-6\right) \\  & =- 2 e^{3} - 4 e + 6.\end{aligned}

Let $C$ be a piecewise-smooth curve given by the vector function $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b].$ Let $f$ be a differentiable function of two or three variables such that $∇f$ is continuous on $C.$ The fundamental theorem for line integrals states that 

$$
{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r=f(r(b))-f(r(a)).
$$

 

In our case, the position vectors of the endpoints of the curve are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨0,0,0⟩ \\ r(1) & =⟨1,2,2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the endpoints of the path defined by $C$ are $(0,0,0)$ and $(1,2,2).$

Applying the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r & =f(r(1))-f(r(0)) \\  & =f(1,2,2)-f(0,0,0) \\  & =\left(- 3 \left(1\right) \left(2\right)^{2} \left(2\right)^{3}\right)-\left(- 3 \left(0\right) \left(0\right)^{2} \left(0\right)^{3}\right) \\  & =\left(-96\right)-\left(0\right) \\  & =-96.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r=f(r(b))-f(r(a)).

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨1,2,1⟩ \\ r(2) & =⟨e^{2},4,e^{-2}⟩.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r & =f(r(2))-f(r(0)) \\  & =f(e^{2},4,e^{-2})-f(1,2,1) \\  & =\left(- \left(e^{2}\right) \left(4\right)^{2} + 3 \left(4\right) \left(e^{-2}\right)\right)-\left(- \left(1\right) \left(2\right)^{2} + 3 \left(2\right) \left(1\right)\right) \\  & =\left(- 16 e^{2} + \frac{12}{e^{2}}\right)-\left(2\right) \\  & =- 16 e^{2} - 2 + \frac{12}{e^{2}}.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

Let $C$ be a piecewise-smooth curve given by the vector function $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b].$ Let $f$ be a differentiable function of two or three variables such that $∇f$ is continuous on $C.$ The fundamental theorem for line integrals states that 

$$
{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r=f(r(b))-f(r(a)).
$$

 

In our case, the position vectors of the endpoints of the curve are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨1,2,1⟩ \\ r(1) & =⟨e,3,e^{-1}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the endpoints of the path defined by $C$ are $(1,2,1)$ and $(e,3,e^{-1}).$

Applying the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r & =f(r(1))-f(r(0)) \\  & =f(e,3,e^{-1})-f(1,2,1) \\  & =\left(- 2 \left(e\right) \left(3\right)^{2} + 2 \left(e\right) \left(3\right) \left(e^{-1}\right)\right)-\left(- 2 \left(1\right) \left(2\right)^{2} + 2 \left(1\right) \left(2\right) \left(1\right)\right) \\  & =\left(6 - 18 e\right)-\left(-4\right) \\  & =10 - 18 e.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Let $f(x,y,z)=- x y^{2} - 2 x y z.$ Given that $C$ is the path along the curve $r(t)=⟨e^{t},t + 3,e^{- t}⟩$ for $t\in [0,2],$ evaluate ${\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $C$ be a piecewise-smooth curve given by the vector function $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b].$ Let $f$ be a differentiable function of two or three variables such that $∇f$ is continuous on $C.$ The fundamental theorem for line integrals states that 

$$
{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r=f(r(b))-f(r(a)).
$$

 

In our case, the position vectors of the endpoints of the curve are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨1,3,1⟩ \\ r(2) & =⟨e^{2},5,e^{-2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the endpoints of the path defined by $C$ are $(1,3,1)$ and $(e^{2},5,e^{-2}).$

Applying the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r & =f(r(2))-f(r(0)) \\  & =f(e^{2},5,e^{-2})-f(1,3,1) \\  & =\left(- \left(e^{2}\right) \left(5\right)^{2} - 2 \left(e^{2}\right) \left(5\right) \left(e^{-2}\right)\right)-\left(- \left(1\right) \left(3\right)^{2} - 2 \left(1\right) \left(3\right) \left(1\right)\right) \\  & =\left(- 25 e^{2} - 10\right)-\left(-15\right) \\  & =5 - 25 e^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$
